column2: The Somakas, struck by arrows loosed from Karna's bow, O king of kings, hid themselves, afflicted by pain and tormented by arrows.
Likewise your army, slain by Nakula's arrows, was scattered in all directions, O king, like clouds driven by the wind.
While the two armies were being slain by the two with great divine arrows, they withdrew out of bowshot and stood like spectators.
When the people had been driven back, the two great-souled warriors, Karna and the Pandava, pierced each other with showers of arrows.
Displaying divine weapons at the head of the battle and suddenly covering each other, each desiring the other's death,
the arrows loosed by Nakula, feathered with heron plumes, covered Karna and stood as before.
Entering houses of arrows, the two were seen by none, O king, like the moon and sun covered at the coming of the rains.
Then Karna, enraged in battle, assuming a more terrible form, covered the Pandava on all sides with showers of arrows.
Covered in battle by the charioteer's son, the Pandava felt no distress, O king, like the sun behind clouds.
Then Adhiratha's son, smiling, sent nets of arrows, O revered one, in hundreds and thousands.
Everything was shadowed by that great soul's arrows, as if covered by clouds by the falling best of arrows.
Then Karna, O great king, cut that great soul's bow and, as if laughing, felled his charioteer from the chariot's seat.
Likewise he swiftly sent his four horses to Yama's abode with four sharp arrows, O Bharata.
Then he quickly shattered his chariot into pieces with arrows, with its banner, wheel-guards, standard, sword, shield marked with a hundred moons, and all equipment.
Horseless, chariotless and without armour, O lord of men, he quickly got down from the chariot and stood grasping an iron club.
The charioteer's son, O king, broke that dreadful raised club with arrows, in hundreds and thousands.
Seeing him weaponless, Karna tormented him many times with straight-jointed arrows, but did not press him to death.
Struck in battle by the stronger one skilled in weapons, Nakula suddenly fled, O king, his senses confused.
Pursuing him, Radheya, laughing again and again, hung his bow, with its string, round his neck, O Bharata.
Then he shone, O king, with the great bow hanging at his neck, like the moon in the sky encircled by a halo, or a white cloud made lovely by the rainbow.
Karna then said to him: "You spoke in vain. Speak now, delighted again—you who are to be slain by me again and again.
Do not fight with the elders and the strong, Pandava; fight your equals, dear one. Feel shame, Pandava, or go home, Madri's son, or to where Krishna and Phalguna are."
Having said this, O great king, he released him; though he was fit to be slain, the charioteer's son did not kill him, remembering Kunti's words, O king, and so released him.
Released by the bowman son of the charioteer, the Pandava, as if ashamed, went to Yudhishthira's chariot.
He mounted the chariot, sighing, scorched by sorrow, like a serpent thrown into a pot, tormented by the charioteer's son.
Having released him in battle, Karna went quickly to the Panchalas on a chariot with many banners and horses the colour of the moon.
There a great lament arose among the Pandavas, O lord of men, on seeing the commander going against throngs of Panchala chariots.
There, O great king, the charioteer's son wrought slaughter, ranging like a wheel at the sun's zenith.
We saw throngs of Panchala chariots carried off—some with broken wheels, their banners and pennants cut, some with their charioteers, some with charioteers slain, and some with broken axles.
Here and there rutting elephants wandered distraught, their limbs seared as in a great forest on fire.
Elephants with split temples, bloodless, trunks cut, bodies torn and tails cut off fell, slain by the great soul, like severed clouds.
Other elephants, terrified by hundreds of iron arrows and javelins, came straight at him like moths into a flame.
Other great elephants were seen groaning, streaming blood from their bodies like mountains with streams of water.
Horses freed from breastplates and tail-bindings, from silver, bronze and golden ornaments,
stripped of blankets and bridles, chowries and cloths, and with quivers fallen,
with their horsemen, heroes who graced the battle, slain, we saw the finest horses wandering in the battle.
We saw horse-warriors in coats and turbans, O lord of men, impaled by lances, swords and spears.
We saw golden-adorned chariots with swift horses well yoked wandering quickly, their warriors slain.
Some had broken axles and poles, others cut wheels, bannerless, with poles and yokes and fittings cut, O revered one.
We saw chariot-warriors there deprived of chariots running in all directions, terrified by the arrows of Surya's son.
Others weaponless, and many armed ones slain of your side, covered with nets, adorned with chest-bells,
adorned with banners of many colours—we saw foot-soldiers running everywhere.
We saw heads, arms and thighs cut off, and others in the battle severed by arrows loosed from Karna's bow.
A great and fearful confusion was seen among the warriors who, driven by Karna's arrows, were slain by sharp shafts.
Slain in battle by the charioteer's son, the Srinjayas came straight at him like moths into a fire.
The kshatriyas avoided that great chariot-warrior burning the divisions here and there, like the raging fire at the end of an age.
The remaining great chariot-warriors of the Panchalas, broken and fleeing, the splendid Karna pursued from behind, scattering arrows, with their armour and banners shattered.
The great chariot-warrior, the charioteer's son, scorched them with arrows, having reached midday like the sun dispelling darkness among beings.
Then, O king, Yuyutsu struck Uluka with a sharp-edged feathered arrow, as Indra strikes a mountain with the thunderbolt.
Uluka, enraged, in the battle cut your son's bow with a razor-arrow and struck him with a karnin arrow.
Casting aside that cut bow, Yuyutsu, his eyes red, took another great and swifter bow.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, he pierced Shakuni's son with sixty arrows, his charioteer with three, and pierced him again.
Uluka, having pierced him with twenty gold-adorned arrows, then, enraged in the battle, cut his golden banner.
Its staff cut, the great banner, gleaming gold, fell shattering in front of Yuyutsu, O king.
Seeing his banner torn down, Yuyutsu, overcome with rage, struck Uluka in the chest with five arrows.
Uluka suddenly cut off with a broad-headed arrow washed in oil the head of his charioteer, O best of the Bharatas.
Having defeated him in battle, O king, Uluka went swiftly on, slaying the Panchalas and Srinjayas with sharp arrows.
Your son Shrutakarman, O great king, made Shatanika's chariot horseless and charioteerless in half a moment, unhurried.
Standing on the chariot whose horses were slain, the mighty Shatanika, enraged, hurled a mace at your son, O revered one.
It reduced the chariot, with its horses and charioteer, to ashes and swiftly fell to earth as if splitting it, O Bharata.
The two heroes, deprived of chariots, increasers of the Kurus' fame, afflicted by the fight, withdrew, looking at one another.
Your son, bewildered, mounted Vivitsu's chariot, and Shatanika swiftly went to Pratívindhya's chariot.
Sutasoma pierced Shakuni with sharp arrows, but could not shake him though enraged, as a flood cannot shake a mountain.
Sutasoma, seeing him as his father's bitter enemy, covered him with many thousands of arrows, O Bharata.
Shakuni, light-handed, a varied fighter, victorious in battle, swiftly cut those arrows with other arrows.
Having warded off those arrows in battle with sharp arrows, he, greatly enraged, struck Sutasoma with three arrows.
Your brother-in-law of great valour shattered his horses, banner and charioteer to bits with arrows, and the people cried out.
Horseless, chariotless and with bow cut, O revered one, the bowman took an excellent bow, stood on the ground from the chariot, and loosed golden-feathered arrows whetted on stone.
They covered your brother-in-law's chariot, flocks of arrows covering the great chariot-warrior like swarms of locusts.
Though he saw them on his chariot-seat, Subala's son, the greatly renowned, was not shaken, crushing those arrows with his own flocks of arrows.
The warriors were delighted there, and the siddhas standing in heaven, seeing that incredible, wondrous deed of Sutasoma, who fought a king on a chariot while himself on foot.
The king cut his bow and all his quiver with sharp, very swift, straight-jointed broad-headed arrows.
With his bow cut in battle, he raised a sword, roaring, bright as lapis lazuli and blue lotus, with ivory hilt.
As he whirled it, shining like spotless sky, the wise Sutasoma seemed like Death itself.
That swordsman suddenly ranged in twenty-four thousand circles, O great king, endowed with strength of training.
Then Subala's valiant son hurled arrows at him, but he swiftly cut them as they came with his excellent sword.
Then, O great king, Subala's son, enraged, slayer of heroes, let fly at Sutasoma arrows like venomous serpents.
He cut them with his sword by skill and strength, displaying his dexterity in battle, with the brilliance of Tarkshya's valour.
As he moved, O king, in his wheeling circles, he cut his bright sword with a very sharp razor-arrow.
Cut off, the great sword suddenly fell to the ground; in his hand remained only the hilt, held powerless.
Knowing the sword to be cut, the great chariot-warrior Sutasoma leapt six paces and hurled the remainder at him.
That cut the bow and string of the great-souled one in battle and swiftly fell to earth, adorned with gold and diamonds; Sutasoma then went to the great chariot-warrior Shrutakirti.
Subala's son too took another dreadful, hard-to-bear bow and advanced against the Pandava army, slaying many hosts of enemies.
There, O lord of men, a great cry arose among the Pandavas on seeing Subala's son moving fearlessly in the battle.
Those proud, armed, great divisions were seen routed by the great-souled son of Subala.
As the king of the gods crushed the daitya host, so Subala's son destroyed the Pandava army.
Kripa held back Dhrishtadyumna in the battle, O king, as a sharabha holds back a proud elephant in the forest.
The Parshata, held by that strong Gautama, could not move a step there, O Bharata.
Seeing Gautama's form facing Dhrishtadyumna's chariot, all beings trembled and thought destruction had come.
There the dejected chariot-warriors and horsemen said, "Surely, at Drona's death, that best of men is enraged.
May Dhrishtadyumna be safe today from Gautama, the Sharadvata of great splendour, knower of divine weapons, noble-minded.
May this whole army be freed from great fear; may this Brahmana not slay all of us assembled here.
The form that is seen, extremely like Death—he will follow Bharadvaja's son's path in battle today.
The preceptor, quick-handed, ever victorious in battle, skilled in weapons, endowed with valour and with anger,
and the Parshata is seen turned back in the fight even now." Such were the various words of your men with the enemy.
Sighing, then, enraged, Kripa Sharadvata, O king, covered the Parshata, leaving him without motion, in all his vital parts.
Struck in battle by the great-souled Gautama, he did not know what to do, bewildered, in that supreme conflict.
His charioteer said to him, "Parshata, are you safe? You have never seen such a calamity in battle.
By fate's arrangement, those arrows aimed at your vital parts by the chief of the twice-born did not pierce them.
I shall turn the chariot back there, as a river's current is turned from the sea. I consider the Brahmana not to be slain, since your valour is spent."
Dhrishtadyumna then said softly, O king, "My mind is bewildered, dear one, and sweat comes on my body.
See the trembling in my body and the hair standing on end; avoid the Brahmana in battle and go slowly to where Achyuta is.
Having reached Arjuna or Bhimasena in battle, charioteer, there will be safety today, driver; that is my firm opinion."
Then, O great king, the charioteer urged the horses and went to where mighty-bowed Bhima was fighting your soldiers.
Seeing Dhrishtadyumna's chariot fleeing, O revered one, Gautama then pursued it, scattering hundreds of arrows.
The tamer of foes blew his conch again and again, and pursued the Parshata who was fleeing, like Mahendra Shambara.
Hardik's son (Kritavarman), as if smiling again and again, held back Shikhandin, the inaccessible cause of Bhishma's death, in the battle.
Shikhandin, approaching the great chariot-warrior of the Hridikas, tormented him in the collarbone with five sharp broad-headed arrows.
Kritavarman, greatly enraged, pierced him with sixty swift arrows and, laughing, O king, cut his bow with one, that great chariot-warrior.
Then Drupada's strong son, taking another bow, enraged, said to Hardikya, "Stand, stand!"
Then he sent ninety golden-feathered, well-whetted arrows at him, O king of kings, but they fell from his armour.
Seeing them useless and fallen on the ground, the strong one cut his bow with a very sharp razor-arrow.
Then, enraged, he tormented him, whose bow was cut like a bull with broken horn, in the arms and chest with eighty arrows.
Kritavarman, greatly enraged and wounded by arrows, taking another bow with a mass of arrows, struck Shikhandin on the shoulder with excellent arrows.
Shikhandin, with arrows lodged in his shoulder, shone like a great tree with spotless spreading branches.
Having pierced each other hard, drenched in blood, they shone like two bulls that have struck each other with their horns.
Striving for each other's death, those two great chariot-warriors ranged there in their chariots in thousands of circles.
Kritavarman, O great king, pierced the Parshata in battle with seventy sharp golden-feathered arrows whetted on stone.
Then the Bhoja, best of strikers, swiftly loosed at him in the battle a dreadful arrow that ends life.
Struck by it, O king, he suddenly fainted and, wrapped in stupor, leant on the flagstaff.
His charioteer carried that best of chariot-warriors out of the battle, tormented by Hardikya's arrows, sighing again and again.
When Drupada's son, the hero, was defeated, the Pandava army, being slain on all sides, fled.
The Trigartas, Shibis with the Kauravas, Shalvas, Samshaptakas and the Narayana force advanced against him.
Satyasena, Satyakirti, Mitradeva, Shrutanjaya, Sushruti, Chitrasena and Mitravarman, O Bharata,
the Trigarta king in battle surrounded by his brothers and by mighty-bowed sons bearing weapons of many kinds,
loosing flights of arrows and showering Arjuna in the fight, rushed at him like floods toward the sea.
Those warriors, hundreds of thousands, coming at Arjuna, all perished, like serpents on seeing Tarkshya.
Though slain in the battle, they did not leave the Pandava, burning like moths in a fire, O king.
Satyasena pierced the Pandava in the battle with three arrows, Mitradeva with sixty-three, and Chandradeva with seven.
Mitravarman with seventy-three, Sushruti with five, Shatrunjaya with twenty, and Susharma with nine arrows.
Having killed King Shatrunjaya with stone-whetted arrows, he struck off Sushruti's head with its helmet from his body, and swiftly sent Chandradeva to Yama's abode with arrows.
Then he held back the other great chariot-warriors who were striving, each with five arrows, O great king.
Satyasena, enraged, hurled a great javelin aimed at Krishna in the battle and roared a lion's roar.
It pierced the left arm of the great-souled Madhava, and then, iron, extremely fierce, fell to the ground.
When Madhava was pierced by the javelin in the great battle, the whip and the reins fell from his hand, O lord of men.
The greatly renowned one, taking up whip and reins again, drove those horses towards Satyasena's chariot.
Seeing Vishvaksena (Krishna) wounded, Partha Dhananjaya, mighty, pierced Satyasena with sharp arrows.
Then with very sharp arrows he severed the great head of that king, adorned with earrings, from his body amid the host.
Having killed him with sharp arrows, he struck Mitravarman, and his charioteer with a sharp calf-tooth arrow, O revered one.
Then, self-controlled, enraged, he felled bands of Samshaptakas with hundreds of arrows, in hundreds and thousands.
Then the greatly renowned one cut off the head of the great-souled king Mitradeva with a silver-feathered razor-arrow, and enraged, struck Sushama in the collarbone.
Then all the Samshaptakas, surrounding Dhananjaya, crushed him with floods of weapons, enraged, making all ten quarters resound.
Tormented by them, Jishnu, equal to Shakra in valour, of immeasurable spirit, the great chariot-warrior, brought forth Indra's weapon; then thousands of arrows appeared, O lord of men.
A great noise was heard here and there of banners being cut, bows in battle, chariots with pennants, quivers with their arrows,
axles, yokes, wheels with their reins, poles, armour, and arrows in the battle,
stones falling, lances with spears, maces, iron clubs, darts with javelins,
shataghnis with wheels, arms with thighs, necklaces and armlets, and bracelets, O revered one,
necklaces and gold ornaments, coats of mail, parasols, fans and heads with crowns.
Heads with earrings, fine eyes and faces like the full moon were seen on the earth like clusters of stars in the sky.
Bodies of the slain with fine garlands and garments, anointed with sandal, were seen on the ground; the dreadful battlefield was like a gandharva city.
The earth was covered with slain princes, mighty kshatriyas, fallen elephants and horses, impassable in battle as if with shattered mountains.
There was no wheel-track for the great-souled Pandava as he killed foes with broad-headed arrows and a great number of elephants and horses.
The chariot wheels sank to the hub, O revered one, as he ranged in that mud of blood.
The horses, swift as thought and wind, yoked with great effort, strongly carried the sinking wheels.
That army, slain by the bowman son of Pandu, mostly turned away and did not stand in battle.
Having defeated in battle those many hosts of Samshaptakas, Jishnu shone, O great king, like a smokeless blazing fire.
King Duryodhana himself fearlessly confronted Yudhishthira, O great king, who was loosing many arrows.
As your mighty son suddenly rushed at him, the king of dharma swiftly pierced him and said, "Stand, stand!"
He pierced him back with nine sharp arrows and, greatly enraged, struck his charioteer hard with a broad-headed arrow.
Then King Yudhishthira hurled at Duryodhana thirteen golden-feathered, stone-whetted arrows.
Having killed his four horses with four, the great chariot-warrior with the fifth struck off the charioteer's head from his body.
With the sixth he cut the king's banner, with the seventh his bow, with the eighth he felled his sword to the ground, and with five the king of dharma tormented the king hard.
Your son, leaping from the chariot whose horses were slain, in the utmost calamity stood on the ground.
Seeing him in distress, Karna, Drona's son, Kripa and others came together, wishing to save the king.
Then all the sons of Pandu surrounded Yudhishthira and advanced in battle, O king, and the fight began.
Then thousands of trumpets sounded in the great battle, with shouts and uproar, O lord of the earth, as the Panchalas advanced with the Kauravas.
Men met men, elephants met the best elephants, chariots met chariot-warriors, and horses met horsemen.
Duels took place, O great king, wondrous to see in the battle, astonishing, inconceivable, with the best weapons.
They fought with great speed, each wishing the other's death; in the battle they killed one another, observing a warrior's vow; they never turned their backs in battle.
That fight was sweet to behold for a moment only; then, O king, it went on like madness, without restraint.
Thinking heaven to be strong and what must be, the king made his resolve in the battle and set out again to fight.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "This deed done by Bhima, Sanjaya, is beyond belief, that my son of ten thousand elephants' strength was felled."
Kings of many countries, gathering from many quarters with your son, have all met their end.
Then, receiving the honour fitting that time, they duly sat around Yudhishthira.
I am your destroyer and the slayer of your friends; I find no peace, seeing you suffering on the ground.
Rise, tiger of the Kurus, and do your next duty. By the duty of a kshatriya, O Kaurava, this earth has been won by you.
Those heroes always went and attended on that king, bowed at his feet, and stood by the king of dharma's wish; kissed on their heads, they did all their work.
Hearing that the Vrishnis had fallen upon one another through the power of the Brahmin's rod and were destroyed, the Pandavas were pained.
Having consecrated King Parikshit to his own kingdom, the eldest Pandava, afflicted by grief, spoke to Subhadra.
Speaking aloud to them he said, "I do not wish for the worlds together with Duryodhana, who was greedy and short-sighted."
